milestones.title: Goldfield proclaimed and town laid out
milestones.detail: After gold was found on the farm Langlaagte, President Kruger declared the area open for public diggings on 20 September 1886. A town was surveyed beside Ferreira's Camp and named Johannesburg.

milestones.title: Health committee and stock exchange
milestones.detail: A health committee, the town's first local authority, was instituted in November 1887, and the Johannesburg Stock Exchange was founded the same year. The camp already held about 3,000 people.

milestones.title: Railway from the Cape reaches the Rand
milestones.detail: The Cape railway reached the Witwatersrand in September 1892. Lines from Lourenço Marques and Durban followed by 1895.
milestones.source: Diana Cammack (1990), The Rand at War, p. 46, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Johannesburg

milestones.title: Braamfontein dynamite explosion
milestones.detail: On 19 February 1896 a train of 55 tons of dynamite exploded in the Braamfontein goods yard, leaving a crater 250 feet long. At least 78 people were killed and 1,500 injured.
milestones.source: John R. Shorten (1970), The Saga of Johannesburg, p. 198, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Johannesburg

milestones.title: British forces occupy the town
milestones.detail: During the Second Boer War, Lord Roberts's troops marched into Johannesburg on 31 May 1900. Nearly 100,000 white residents had fled the district in the months before the war.
milestones.source: Diana Cammack (1990), The Rand at War, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Johannesburg

milestones.title: Plague scare: Brickfields burned
milestones.detail: In April 1904 the council burned down the Brickfields slum after a plague scare and moved most of its African residents far out of town to Klipspruit, later called Pimville.

milestones.title: Electric trams begin running
milestones.detail: Electric trams began operating in 1906, replacing the horse-drawn tramway of 1891.

milestones.title: Rand Revolt and a university
milestones.detail: White miners' strikes from January to March 1922 turned into an armed revolt, with strikers holding Fordsburg and Jeppe. On 1 March 1922 the University of the Witwatersrand received full university status.

milestones.title: Johannesburg gains city status
milestones.detail: Private Ordinance No. 15 of 1928 of the Transvaal Provincial Council turned the Town of Johannesburg into the City of Johannesburg.

milestones.title: Empire Exhibition
milestones.detail: The Empire Exhibition opened on 15 September 1936 and ran until January 1937. The 1936 census counted over half a million people in the city.

milestones.title: South-western townships named Soweto
milestones.detail: After a naming competition launched in 1959, the council's vast African housing area south-west of the city was given the name Soweto.

milestones.title: Carlton Centre completed
milestones.detail: The fifty-storey Carlton Centre office tower opened as the tallest building in Africa, the peak of a high-rise boom in the central business district.

milestones.title: Soweto uprising
milestones.detail: On 16 June 1976 about 20,000 school students marched in Soweto against teaching in Afrikaans. Police opened fire and the protests spread across the country.

milestones.title: Seat of the new Gauteng province
milestones.detail: With the end of apartheid, Johannesburg became the capital of the new province of Gauteng.

milestones.title: Single metropolitan municipality created
milestones.detail: The City of Johannesburg Metropolitan Municipality was created in 2000, putting the city and its neighbouring municipalities under one council. Soweto became part of the city in 2002.

milestones.title: World Cup final and Gautrain
milestones.detail: The rebuilt Soccer City (FNB Stadium) hosted the 2010 FIFA World Cup final. The Gautrain rapid rail link to Sandton, the airport and Pretoria, begun in 2006, was completed in June 2012.

landmarks.note: 269 m to the top of the antenna spire; the top floor is at 204 m.

landmarks.name: Carlton Centre
landmarks.note: CTBUH gives an architectural height of 201.2 m. Wikipedia and most popular sources give 223 m.

landmarks.name: Nelson Mandela Bridge (north pylon)
landmarks.note: Cable-stayed bridge 284 m long, opened 20 July 2003; the north pylon is 42 m and the south pylon 27 m.

notes: Start date: 1886 is well documented and not contested. The goldfield was proclaimed on 20 September 1886 and the 1911 Britannica dates the town's founding to September 1886; the first tents at Ferreira's Camp went up a little earlier that year. The area had earlier Iron Age and Boer farm occupation but no town. Population: nine points before 1950. The 1887 and 1890 figures are contemporary estimates. The censuses of 1896, 1904, 1908, 1911, 1936 and 1946 use different areas (three-mile radius, municipal area, urban area, city proper), which is stated on each point; 1904 has two published figures (99,022 for the city proper, 155,642 for the municipal area) and the municipal one is used. No figure was found for the 1921 census, so 1911-1936 is covered only by a 1919 estimate. The 1946 city figure excludes much of the African township population counted in the urban agglomeration (762,910). Landmarks: the ten entries all date from 1962 or later. No sourced height was found for the early city's buildings, so these were left out: the Old Fort (1899), Rissik Street Post Office (1897), City Hall (1914), Corner House, Anstey's Building, Escom House (1937, demolished), Ellis Park and FNB Stadium. Wikipedia gives the Rissik Street Post Office a height of 102 m, which cannot be right for a four-storey building and was not used. Skyscraper heights follow CTBUH, which differs from Wikipedia for the Carlton Centre (201.2 m against 223 m) and The Leonardo (227.9 m against 234 m). Coordinates are from Wikipedia and OpenStreetMap. The 2000 date for the metropolitan municipality follows the Wikipedia timeline; another Wikipedia article says 2002.
